title: Phase 5: Validation, error handling and API contracts
description: Implement FluentValidation pipeline behavior for command validation, ASP.NET Core ProblemDetails for consistent error responses, and a shared Result<T> pattern that preserves error context from domain to transport layer.

data.text: A well-designed API contract is a form of documentation that never gets stale. When every endpoint returns the same envelope and every error follows RFC 7807 (ProblemDetails), clients can build predictable error UIs without reading your wiki.

Instead of throwing exceptions for business rule violations (which obscures the control flow and leaks stack traces), handlers return Result<T>. Success carries the value; Failure carries a list of human-readable errors.

data.title: C#: Result<T> discriminated type
data.content: A sealed record type gives you exhaustive pattern matching in C#.

data.text: Validators run before the handler executes. If validation fails, the pipeline short-circuits and returns a 422 with a list of errors. Domain exceptions that slip through the validator are caught by a second behavior and mapped to 400/422.

data.title: C#: Validation pipeline behavior
data.content: Generic IPipelineBehavior<,> lets MediatR intercept every command.

data.title: C#: SubmitExpenseReportValidator with FluentValidation
data.content: Validators enforce shape and business rules before hitting the domain.

data.text: ASP.NET Core 8+ includes ProblemDetails support out of the box. We register a custom exception handler to map DomainException, ValidationException, and NotFoundException to consistent RFC 7807 responses.

data.title: C#: Global exception handler with ProblemDetails
data.content: Keep error schemas consistent so the React app can build a single ErrorBanner component.

data.title: Never return stack traces to the client
data.text: In production, GenericProblemDetails should strip Type and any internal exception details. Log the full exception server-side; return only Title and Detail to the client.

Contract changes are inevitable. Use media type versioning (e.g., `application/vnd.expense.v1+json`) or URL versioning (`/api/v1/expense-reports`) from day one. Avoid silent breaking changes — if you must change a DTO, bump the version and support both during migration.

items.text: Result<T> type implemented with Success and Failure factory methods.
ValidationPipelineBehavior registered globally; failing requests return 422 before hitting the handler.
SubmitExpenseReportValidator covers all business rules (amounts, dates, item count).
All API responses include the standard ProblemDetails envelope in development.
At least one contract test proving the submit endpoint returns the expected JSON schema.

data.title: Phase 5 summary
points: Result<T> removes exception-driven control flow from handlers.
FluentValidation + pipeline behavior keeps validators co-located with commands.
ProblemDetails provides a standard error envelope clients can rely on.
API versioning from day one prevents painful breaking-change migrations later.
data.takeaway: Consistent error responses are a product feature, not an afterthought. A frontend engineer building an ErrorBanner component will thank you for a stable, documented contract.

furtherReading.title: RFC 7807: Problem Details for HTTP APIs
